subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 50 minutes × 10 periods = 500 minutes
Total: 10 periods · 8h 20min

periods.activity_title: Elderly in Our Lives: Activating and First Reading

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reflect and Respond (p.97): graphic organiser on elderly care, paired class discussion.
Reflect and Respond (p.97): share a tradition or recipe passed down by an elderly relative.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the chapter title and the concept of 'Vitamin-M'. Students brainstorm what the phrase might mean and share initial guesses aloud.

Students individually complete the graphic organiser from Reflect and Respond (p.97) — four prompts on caring for the elderly, their challenges, reasons, and solutions. Pairs then exchange and discuss their responses with each other.

Whole-class discussion on the graphic organiser. Teacher draws out common threads: dignity, independence, forgetfulness. Students then respond to the prompt about a family tradition or recipe passed down by an elderly person, sharing briefly in pairs.
Teacher reads aloud the opening paragraphs of 'Vitamin-M' (p.97–99), with students following in their textbooks. Class notices the narrator's tone and Grandpa's rocking chair scene.

periods.teacher_notes: The graphic organiser works best if students are given genuine thinking time before sharing — rushing straight to discussion produces surface responses. The opening scene where Vidya wishes someone would invent a memory pill while Grandpa sits quietly listening sets up the story's central irony; drawing attention to it during the read-aloud plants a question students carry into the reading. An unanchored vocabulary-awareness task (p.98, word-familiarity table) is available for self-study: students may explore words such as 'frail', 'poky', and 'pottering' using a dictionary at home.
materials: Blank paper or printed graphic organiser template

periods.activity_title: Reading Section I: Grandpa Arrives, Ravi's Dilemma

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Check Your Understanding (p.102): four short-answer questions on Grandpa's city dislike, Vidya's fears, Ravi's attitude, and the promise.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads aloud pp.99–102 of 'Vitamin-M' with expression, assigning Grandpa's and Vidya's dialogue to student volunteers. Students follow in their textbooks, noting Grandpa's mahogany walking stick and his ten years of independent living.
Students re-read pp.99–102 silently with a focus question: 'What does Grandpa value most, and what has he lost?' Teacher circulates and prompts students who are stuck.

Students respond in writing to the four Check Your Understanding questions (p.102). Teacher takes brief answers aloud, correcting misreadings — especially the nuance that Ravi sympathises with Grandpa even while nominally keeping his mother's rules.
Quick pair exchange: 'Would you have made the same promise Ravi made?' Students share one sentence each. Teacher closes by noting that Grandpa's craftiness will drive the next episode.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often read Vidya as simply harsh; the guided-reading phase should surface that she acts from fear following real incidents — an accidental double medicine dose and Grandpa lying outside all night after a fall. The four comprehension questions reward careful reading rather than impression; encourage students to quote a word or phrase from the text in each answer.

periods.activity_title: Comedy of Errors: Grandpa's Day Out

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Check Your Understanding (p.106): flow chart — seven blanks describing Grandpa's day out.
Check Your Understanding (p.107): three questions — Grandpa lost?, Ravi's feeling, mother's knowledge.

time_bands.activity: Shared reading of pp.102–107: teacher and volunteers alternate paragraphs. The comic episodes — elephant bush, banyan tree, Ladies' Hairdressing Salon — are read with attention to Ravi's mounting embarrassment and Grandpa's oblivious enjoyment.

Students complete the seven-blank flow chart (p.106) individually, tracing Grandpa's route and Ravi's mishaps. Teacher draws the flow chart outline on the board and invites students to fill it in collaboratively.
Class discusses the three follow-up questions (p.107): Was Grandpa lost? How did Ravi feel? Will Vidya find out? Students give brief spoken answers; teacher encourages inference rather than summary.
Teacher poses a discussion hook: 'Grandpa bought banned food and gave away his cap — is this irresponsible or understandable?' Students hold that thought for the next reading.

periods.teacher_notes: The comedy in this section depends on the reader tracking two simultaneous journeys — Grandpa's confident strolling and Ravi's frantic ducking. During the flow chart, students sometimes confuse who is scolded or where; direct them back to the vendor scene and the Ladies' Salon episode in the text. Ravi's bus error — following the bald stranger wearing Grandpa's yellow cap — is the story's comic peak and worth a brief re-read aloud.
materials: Blackboard or whiteboard for flow chart

periods.activity_title: The Birthday Twist: Close Reading and Character Insight

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Check Your Understanding (p.109): three questions on Ravi's emotional reaction, Grandpa's gift-giving habit, and the detective-book gift.
Critical Reflection (p.109–110): Extract 1 — five sub-questions on Grandpa's nostalgia and the brick-house passage.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads aloud pp.107–109 (the homecoming and birthday reveal) with students following. The moment Grandpa says 'I had a quiet morning' is re-read twice so students feel the irony of his words.
Students answer the three Check Your Understanding questions (p.109) in writing. Teacher takes answers aloud and probes: 'What word in the text shows Ravi felt relieved rather than just confused?'

Close reading of Extract 1 from Critical Reflection (p.109–110): the brick-house passage. Students read the extract, then work through all five sub-questions — emotion identification, sentence completion, reason for city move, idiom meaning, and advantage/disadvantage — individually before a brief class share.
Quick oral reflection: 'Which one word best describes Grandpa — nostalgic, dignified, or crafty? Justify in one sentence.' Students respond in pairs.

periods.teacher_notes: The critical distinction in Extract 1 is between 'nostalgic' and 'wistful' — students benefit from a brief discussion of how both describe longing but nostalgic is backward-looking while wistful can be generalised yearning. Grandpa's gift of 'The Best Detective Stories' to Ravi is the story's sharpest moment of wit; if the class has not yet seen the irony, pause and re-read the wink.

periods.activity_title: Critical Reflection: Character, Memory, and Age Bias

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Critical Reflection (p.110–111): Extract 2 — five sub-questions on Grandpa's tone, Ravi's embarrassment, and the reported-speech sequence.
Critical Reflection II (p.111): eight analytical questions — character traits, memory, age bias, Vitamin-M ownership.

homework.task_brief: Critical Reflection II (p.111): questions 5, 7, and 8 — Ravi as detective, who needs Vitamin-M, and age discrimination example — for extended written response.

time_bands.activity: Students read Extract 2 (p.110–111) and work through its five sub-questions individually: tone of Grandpa's reply, reason for Ravi's embarrassment, fill-in on Vidya's impatience, true/false on the birthday, and Grandpa's knowing comment. Teacher reviews answers whole-class, pausing on the true/false item — Grandpa clearly did not forget.

Class works through Critical Reflection II questions 1–4 and 6 together: disproving the 'failing memory' claim with two textual evidences, character traits of all three characters, Ravi's tea-stall worry, difficulty of tailing Grandpa, and evidence that Grandpa knew he was being followed. Students write answers in their notebooks, then share.

Teacher-led discussion on question 8 — age discrimination: when are people's opinions dismissed because of age, young or old? Students share a brief personal observation. Teacher notes the story's critique of Vidya's assumptions about Grandpa's competence.

periods.teacher_notes: Question 1 of Critical Reflection II (p.111) asks for evidence that Grandpa's memory is sharp — point students to his encyclopaedic chess knowledge, his systematic birthday gift-giving, and his cool recall of exactly what Ravi did all morning. Questions 5, 7, and 8 require extended personal response and work better as written homework where students have time to develop an argument.

periods.activity_title: Movement, Sound, and Word-Building in Context

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.112): classify movement vs. sound words; fill ten blanks in the Detective Shankar passage.
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.113): two synonym-puzzle blanks for DILEMMA using a dictionary.
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.113): complete four-column table for six story words — meaning, part of speech, synonym, antonym.

time_bands.activity: Students sort the twenty story words (p.112) into movement and sound columns individually, then compare in pairs. Whole-class check on the board. Students then use words from their columns to fill in the ten blanks of the Detective Shankar passage, reading it aloud when complete.

Students solve the two synonym-puzzle blanks for 'dilemma' (p.113) — QUANDARY and PREDICAMENT — using a dictionary if needed. Teacher highlights that all three words share the 'stuck between two options' sense but differ in register.

Students complete the four-column vocabulary table (p.113) for craftily, dilemma, furious, boomed, humiliation, and attire — meaning, part of speech, synonym, antonym — consulting their dictionaries. Teacher elicits answers and corrects part-of-speech labels aloud.
Quick oral round: teacher says a story word from the table and a student must give one synonym and one antonym from memory. Fast-paced and lightly competitive.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often misclassify 'bustle' and 'evicted' — 'bustle' is a movement/activity word here, while 'evicted' is movement. Confirming context in the story passage helps. The synonym-puzzle format (partially revealed letters) supports dictionary use without giving the answer away; ensure students record full dictionary entries, not just the answer word.

periods.activity_title: Prepositions and Reported Speech: Grammar in Action

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.113): match five emotion words to meanings with one extra option.
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.114): identify prepositions in four story phrases; fill six blanks in the passage.
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.114–116): interrogative sentence types and reported-speech transformation — Arvind–Priya conversation, six blanks.

time_bands.activity: Students match five emotion/expression words (embarrassed, countered, flushed, stricken, gleam) to their meanings (p.113), noting that one meaning is extra. Answers are reviewed aloud with teacher noting how these words appear at emotional peaks in the story.

Students underline prepositions in the four story phrases (p.114) and fill in the six-blank passage using the given preposition options. Teacher models the first blank, then students work individually. Class reviews answers with attention to how prepositions of place (across, behind, under) drive Ravi's surveillance comedy.

Teacher leads the interrogative-sentence analysis (p.114–115): four guided questions on exclamatory vs. interrogative, Wh-type vs. Yes/No type. Students then study the direct-to-indirect speech table and transform the Arvind–Priya conversation (p.116) into reported speech, filling six blanks.
Students read out two of their reported-speech transformations aloud. Teacher highlights the key pronoun and tense shifts required.

periods.teacher_notes: The reported-speech section at p.114–116 is the most grammatically dense part of this chapter; students who have worked with direct and indirect speech before will move quickly through the four guided questions and need more time on the Arvind–Priya transformation. The preposition exercise is grounded in the story's physical chase scenes, so inviting students to locate the original phrases in the text before completing the blanks reinforces contextual understanding.

periods.activity_title: Meditation Podcast and Intonation in Questions

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Listen and Respond (p.116–117): podcast on meditation — complete five sentence-completion blanks with exact words.
Speaking Activity (p.117): intonation patterns in questions — study examples, revisit story questions, practise aloud in pairs.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the meditation podcast transcript aloud twice at a measured pace, pausing between sentences (p.266, baked into summary). On the first listening students simply follow; on the second they complete the five sentence-completion items (p.116–117) using no more than three exact words per blank.

Class reviews the five answers together. Teacher explains the connection: the podcast discusses meditation's role in well-being and memory — a thematic echo of the story's concern with mental sharpness and Vitamin-M.

Students study the five intonation pattern examples on p.117 — falling (Wh), rising (Yes/No), rising (affirmative + negative tag), falling (negative + affirmative tag), rise-fall (choice). They then revisit the story text and select two or three questions, practising them aloud in pairs with the correct intonation pattern.
Three or four volunteers read their chosen story question aloud to the class; classmates identify the intonation pattern used. Teacher provides brief feedback.

periods.teacher_notes: For the listening task, playing the transcript as a read-aloud (rather than a recording) is the standard classroom practice; two readings with a brief pause between them give students adequate time to write. The intonation exercise works best when students select questions that genuinely differ in pattern — teacher can prompt pairs who have chosen two similar types to look for a tag question or choice question in the story.

periods.activity_title: Personal Narrative Presentation and Magazine Article Draft

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Speaking Activity (p.117): structured oral presentation on a personal caregiving experience — four guided prompts.
Writing Task (p.117): four-paragraph magazine article 'Our Inspiring Elderly' — draft, peer response, and revise within the unit.

time_bands.activity: Three or four students deliver their prepared oral presentations on a personal caregiving experience (p.117), structured around the four prompts: background, what they learned about themselves, understanding the older person's needs, and insights into aging. After each, one classmate offers a brief observation on what was expressed well.

Teacher models the four-paragraph structure for the magazine article 'Our Inspiring Elderly' on the board: introduction, details and examples, challenges overcome, and concluding comment. Students note the title, name, and grade format.

Students draft all four paragraphs of the article individually in their notebooks. Teacher circulates, prompting students who stall at the introduction to begin with a specific detail or anecdote from Grandpa or their own experience.
Pairs exchange drafts and give one compliment and one specific suggestion for improvement. Students make one revision to their draft based on the feedback before the end of the unit.

periods.teacher_notes: The speaking presentations should be brief — a quick paired exchange rather than a formal address — so all four bands have time. The article drafting, peer response, and revision are all contained within this unit; no draft is carried forward. Students sometimes write only a single long paragraph; the four-paragraph scaffold on the board prevents this.

periods.activity_title: Beyond the Text: Memory, Family Albums, and The Lost Child

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Learning Beyond the Text (p.118): identify the correct image of Grandpa's walking stick from four options.
Learning Beyond the Text (p.120–125): read and discuss 'The Lost Child' by Mulk Raj Anand — compare themes of attachment and parental authority with Vitamin-M.

homework.task_brief: Learning Beyond the Text (p.118–119): collect family photographs and prepare a slide show — when, where, who, and why memorable.

time_bands.activity: Students revisit the story's description of Grandpa's walking stick — mahogany, brass handle carved as an eagle's head — and identify the correct image (p.118) from four options. Brief class confirmation and discussion of why visual details matter in characterisation.

Teacher reads aloud key passages of 'The Lost Child' (pp.120–125), with students following. Students note the contrast: the child suppresses every desire when with his parents, then rejects all the same things once lost — wanting only his parents back.

Comparative discussion: how does the child's attachment in 'The Lost Child' compare to Ravi's quiet loyalty to Grandpa in 'Vitamin-M'? Both texts show that the relationship matters more than the object of desire. Students share observations in a teacher-facilitated open exchange.

Teacher introduces the slide-show homework task (p.118–119): students will collect a few memorable family photographs and prepare a short slide show noting when, where, who, and why each is memorable. This is set as independent work for outside the unit.

periods.teacher_notes: The walking-stick image task sharpens close reading of descriptive prose — the brass eagle-head handle is mentioned twice in the story and students who have read carefully will locate the correct image quickly. The comparison between 'The Lost Child' and 'Vitamin-M' is productive because both pivot on what a child truly values in a caregiving relationship; teacher need not resolve the comparison but should ensure students articulate at least one concrete parallel.

items.source_lo: Student analyses character motivation, intergenerational conflict, and authorial use of irony and comic detail using prose as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Grandpa's covert day out, Ravi's failed surveillance, and the birthday-twist revelation exposing age bias.
items.item_stem: In the story, Vidya locks up Grandpa's house and brings him to the city against his wishes. Which of the following best explains Vidya's motivation for doing this?

options.label: A
options.text: She believed Grandpa was incapable of managing his own finances.

options.label: B
options.text: She needed Grandpa's help in looking after Ravi during school holidays.

options.label: C
options.text: She wanted Grandpa to enjoy the comforts and entertainment of city life.

options.label: D
options.text: She was concerned for his safety after a series of accidents when he lived alone.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Chooser has confused Grandpa's perspective (he hates city bustle) with Vidya's actual reason.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Chooser has inferred a financial concern not stated in the text; the accidents, not finances, drive Vidya.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Chooser has reversed the relationship — Vidya instructs Ravi to look after Grandpa, not the other way around.

items.source_lo: Student analyses character motivation, intergenerational conflict, and authorial use of irony and comic detail using prose as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Grandpa's covert day out, Ravi's failed surveillance, and the birthday-twist revelation exposing age bias.
items.item_stem:
Read the passage below and answer the questions that follow.

1. What does Grandpa's parting comment — telling Vidya that Ravi had 'disappeared instead of staying at home to look after me like you told him to' — reveal about his awareness of the day's events? Support your answer with one detail from the story.
2. Grandpa gives Ravi a copy of The Best Detective Stories as a birthday gift and winks. Explain the irony in this choice of gift, and what it suggests about Grandpa's view of Ravi's actions.
3. The narrator describes Grandpa as 'coolly' delivering his account of the morning. Analyse how this single adverb shapes the reader's understanding of the power balance between Grandpa and the rest of the family.
items.visual_stimulus: "I had a quiet morning, but I don't know about Ravi. He just disappeared instead of staying at home to look after me like you told him to," answered Grandpa coolly, while Ravi just looked confused and embarrassed. Grandpa had another surprise for Ravi. A gift-wrapped parcel! "But, Papa, Ravi's birthday was three months ago. Have you forgotten?" exclaimed Ravi's mother, impatiently. Grandpa smiled and held out the parcel. "I always give gifts on my birthday," he said. "And today is my birthday."

expected_elements: Grandpa is fully aware Ravi followed him; his comment is deliberate, not accidental.
The detective-story gift mocks Ravi's surveillance while showing affectionate wit.
The adverb 'coolly' signals Grandpa's composure and control over the narrative.
Grandpa turns the tables: the supposed 'child' outmanoeuvres the supposed 'adults'.
Together, questions reveal Grandpa's sharp memory and dignified assertion of autonomy.

items.source_lo: Student listens to a spoken informational text and extracts key details accurately using note-taking from listening as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Podcast on meditation — its benefits for well-being, memory, stress reduction, and daily routine.
items.item_stem:
Listen to the meditation podcast. Then decide whether each of the following statements is true or false, and write one word or phrase from the podcast that justifies your answer.
(1) Meditation removes stress-causing thoughts and thereby improves emotional and physical well-being.
(2) According to the podcast, meditation is recommended only for students facing examination pressure.
(3) The speaker says that regular meditation can help people manage challenging situations with ease.

options.text: According to the podcast, meditation is recommended only for students facing examination pressure.
Meditation removes stress-causing thoughts and thereby improves emotional and physical well-being.
The speaker says that regular meditation can help people manage challenging situations with ease.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (1) True — justified by 'all kinds of thoughts which cause stress are removed, resulting in an enhanced state of well-being, both physically and emotionally'. (2) False — the podcast recommends daily meditation for everyone's overall well-being, not only for exam-stressed students. (3) True — justified by 'allowing you to manage challenges with ease'.

items.source_lo: Student listens to a spoken informational text and extracts key details accurately using note-taking from listening as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Podcast on meditation — its benefits for well-being, memory, stress reduction, and daily routine.
items.item_stem:
After listening to the podcast, a student makes the following notes. Two of the blanks are incorrect — the student misheard the podcast. Identify which two are wrong and write the correct information from the podcast.

Note 1: Meditation provides rest and peace to the body.
Note 2: After meditation a person gains a new perspective on stressful situations.
Note 3: Meditation helps to reduce negative emotions.
Note 4: The speaker says meditation improves exam scores directly.
Note 5: The speaker encourages making meditation a daily routine.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Note 1 is incorrect — the podcast says meditation provides rest and peace to the mind, not the body. Note 4 is incorrect — the podcast says daily meditation can help lessen exam-related pressure, not that it improves exam scores directly.

items.source_lo: Student uses intonation and structured oral narration to convey personal experience and engage an audience using oral presentation as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Intonation patterns in questions from the story; personal caregiving experience structured around aging and dignity.
items.item_stem: Read the following question from the story aloud to a partner: 'You didn't tell him to stay at home and look after me, did you?' Identify the intonation pattern this question follows — rising or falling on the question tag — and explain in one sentence why that pattern is used here. Then read the question again to your partner with the correct intonation.

expected_elements: Student correctly identifies the falling intonation on the negative main clause with affirmative tag.
Student can explain that falling intonation on the tag signals the speaker expects confirmation.
Student's read-aloud demonstrates the fall on 'did you' rather than a rising lilt.
Explanation is given in one clear sentence without reading from notes.

items.source_lo: Student uses intonation and structured oral narration to convey personal experience and engage an audience using oral presentation as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Intonation patterns in questions from the story; personal caregiving experience structured around aging and dignity.
items.item_stem: In the story, Vidya believes she must protect Grandpa by restricting his independence, while Grandpa insists his freedom and dignity are equally important. Argue, with reasons, which position you find more convincing. Your argument should: name the position you support, give two reasons drawn from the story or your own experience, and respond to one point the opposing side might make.

expected_elements: Student states a clear position — safety-first or autonomy-first — at the outset.
Two reasons are given, at least one grounded in story details (accidents, Grandpa's self-management).
Student acknowledges and counters one argument from the opposing view.
Argument is delivered in organized, audible speech without reading a script.
Student uses appropriate persuasive language — 'I believe', 'on the other hand', 'this shows'.

items.source_lo: Student drafts a structured magazine article using guided writing to organise ideas, examples, and a concluding comment in formal prose.
items.source_context: Article for a school magazine advocating for recognition of elderly people's wisdom and contributions to society.
items.item_stem: Your school's student magazine is publishing a special issue on community bonds. Write a notice of no more than 60 words for the school notice board inviting students to contribute articles, photographs, or short stories about memorable time spent with an older family member or neighbour. Include the submission deadline, the person to contact, and one sentence on why these stories matter to the school community.

expected_elements: Notice follows standard format: heading, body, and name/designation of issuing authority.
Submission deadline and contact person are both clearly stated.
One sentence articulates why intergenerational stories matter to the community.
Word count stays within approximately 60 words.
Formal, clear language appropriate to a school notice board.

items.source_lo: Student drafts a structured magazine article using guided writing to organise ideas, examples, and a concluding comment in formal prose.
items.source_context: Article for a school magazine advocating for recognition of elderly people's wisdom and contributions to society.
items.item_stem: A reader of your school magazine has written a letter arguing that older people in families should follow the rules set by younger family members because 'times have changed and the elderly cannot keep up'. Write a letter to the editor (120–150 words) agreeing or disagreeing with this view. Use at least one specific reason and address one point the original letter made.

expected_elements: Letter-to-editor format used: date, editor's address, salutation, and sign-off.
Student clearly states agreement or disagreement in the opening paragraph.
At least one specific reason is given, relevant to the theme of autonomy and dignity.
The original letter's claim is directly acknowledged and countered or supported.
Formal register maintained throughout; word count within 120–150 words.

items.source_lo: Student identifies and applies movement and sound vocabulary, prepositions, and reported-speech transformation using grammar-in-context from a prose narrative as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Story vocabulary of action and sensation; prepositions of place in chase scenes; interrogative and reported speech from character dialogue.
items.item_stem:
The sentences below are taken from a conversation between Ravi and his mother about the morning's events. Rewrite each sentence in reported speech, making all necessary changes to pronouns, tense, and question structure.

(a) Ravi's mother asked Ravi, "Where did you go this morning?"
(b) Ravi said, "Grandpa went out and I tried to follow him."
(c) His mother asked him, "Will you tell me exactly what happened?"
(d) Ravi replied, "I have already told you everything I know."

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (a) Ravi's mother asked Ravi where he had gone that morning. (b) Ravi said that Grandpa had gone out and he had tried to follow him. (c) His mother asked him whether he would tell her exactly what had happened. (d) Ravi replied that he had already told her everything he knew.

items.source_context: Comparison of Ravi's loyalty to Grandpa in Vitamin-M with the child's bond in The Lost Child by Mulk Raj Anand.
items.item_stem: In 'The Lost Child' by Mulk Raj Anand, the child eagerly wants sweets, toys, and a roundabout ride while at the fair with his parents, but holds back each time. Once separated from his parents, he rejects all the same attractions offered by a kind stranger. What does this shift reveal about what the child truly values? Write your answer in 3–4 sentences.

expected_elements: Student identifies that the child values the relationship with his parents above all objects of desire.
Student explains that the desires were suppressed by parental authority, not absent.
Student notes the shift: once lost, security matters more than any attraction.
Student uses a specific detail from the story — sweets, roundabout, or the stranger's offer.
Response is written in 3–4 organised sentences.

items.source_lo: Student compares themes of attachment, parental authority, and intergenerational bonds across two prose texts using comparative study as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Comparison of Ravi's loyalty to Grandpa in Vitamin-M with the child's bond in The Lost Child by Mulk Raj Anand.
items.item_stem: Design a project that places 'Vitamin-M' and 'The Lost Child' in conversation with each other. Your project outline should: (a) name one shared theme across both stories and explain it in 2–3 sentences; (b) identify one key difference in how each story treats the relationship between a child and an older or parental figure; and (c) describe one way you would present this comparison to an audience — for example, a short illustrated booklet, a poster, a short script, or a multimedia slide show — and explain why that format suits the comparison.

expected_elements: A shared theme is named (attachment, parental authority, or what children truly value) and explained with reference to both texts.
One meaningful difference is identified — e.g. Ravi acts independently while the lost child is helpless; Grandpa is an adult authority while the fair parents are young adults.
A presentation format is chosen and its suitability explained in at least one sentence.
Project outline is coherent and draws on specific story details from both texts.
Response demonstrates analytical thinking, not mere summary of both plots.
